q: How does a sentence embedding model work?
a: A Transformer encoder reads the text and its token vectors are pooled into one vector. It's trained contrastively on (query, relevant passage) pairs with in-batch negatives, so related texts get high cosine similarity.

q: Can you use different embedding models for documents and queries?
a: No. Each model has its own vector space; distances across models are meaningless. Use the same model and version, and re-embed everything when you switch.

q: Cosine vs dot product vs Euclidean distance?
a: Cosine measures angle, ignoring length; dot product includes length; L2 measures straight-line distance. For unit-normalised vectors all three give the same ranking (\(\|a-b\|^2 = 2 - 2a\cdot b\)). Use what the embedding model was trained for.

Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a multi-layer graph where each vector links to nearby vectors. Search starts at a sparse top layer, greedily hops toward the query, and descends to denser layers. Fast with high recall; tuned with M (links per node), efConstruction and efSearch; uses a lot of memory.

HNSW: graph-based, very fast and accurate, memory-hungry. IVF-PQ: cluster vectors (IVF) and search only the nearest clusters, with vectors compressed by product quantisation; far less memory, somewhat lower recall. Choose by scale, memory budget and recall target.

q: How do you pick an embedding model?
a: Check MTEB retrieval scores for your language and domain, then test on your own question set (recall@k). Consider max input length, dimension (storage), latency, cost, multilingual needs, and whether it can be hosted where your data must stay.

q: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering in vector search?
a: Post-filtering retrieves top-k by similarity and then drops items that fail the metadata filter, which can leave too few results. Pre-filtering restricts the search to items that pass the filter first, which is correct but harder to do efficiently with ANN indexes. Good vector DBs support filtered search natively.

A Transformer encoder with pooling is fine-tuned with contrastive loss on (query, relevant passage) pairs: pull each query towards its passage and push it away from in-batch and hard negatives, essentially a softmax over 'which passage is the right one'.

q: You switched embedding models. What else must change?
a: Re-embed and re-index every chunk: vectors from different models live in different spaces and can't be compared. Store the model name/version with the index and re-run retrieval evaluation.

q: What are the key HNSW parameters?
a: M (links per node; more = better recall, more memory), ef_construction (build quality) and ef_search (candidates explored per query; higher = better recall, slower).
